x5.h: The 2024 specimen Paper 1: a second look at the format
p: Cambridge publishes a specimen paper to show exactly how Paper 1 looks for examination from 2024. A specimen is a model. It is not a past exam, but it has the same structure, marks and mark scheme style. The specimen Paper 1 has 17 questions and 60 marks, in six exercises.
• Exercise 1, Questions 1 to 6, 8 marks: a short article about living stone plants. Five one-mark questions and one three-mark question asking for advice.
• Exercise 2, Question 7(a) to (i), 9 marks: matching nine statements to texts.
• Exercise 3, Questions 8 and 9, 7 marks: notes about tiny homes. Three marks for disadvantages and four for reasons they are popular.
• Exercise 4, Questions 10 to 15, 6 marks: six multiple-choice questions.
• Exercise 5, Question 16, 15 marks: an informal email about a problem with something bought online.
• Exercise 6, Question 17, 15 marks: a report on a sports festival, using four student comments as prompts.
Use the specimen with your students in the first month to show them what the paper looks like. You will study its answers and lessons in Unit 27 in Week 4.

b: It matches the new format.
It has a full mark scheme with the generic marking principles.
It is a safe way to practise without using up past papers.

x6.h: Six key messages from the June 2024 examiner report
p: The Principal Examiner Report for Teachers, June 2024, begins each Paper 1 report with key messages for teachers. Here they are in simple words. Share them with your students.
• In Exercises 1 to 4: underline or highlight the central focus of each question, to be sure that every part is answered and to avoid adding wrong details.
• In Exercise 1: do not add incorrect information to a correct answer. Give a precise answer, with no excess details.

• In Exercise 2: think about the message of each paragraph. The answer often depends on following words that join sentences (discourse markers), not only one key word or synonym. Many students find questions on implied meaning hard.
• In Exercise 3: put the notes under the correct heading. Notes should be brief and give only key details.
• In Exercise 4: the details in each option, A, B and C, will be mentioned in the text. But only one option fully and accurately matches the main focus of the question.

• In Exercises 5 and 6: develop the answer as fully as possible and complete the task. In Exercise 5 all three bullet points must be addressed. In Exercise 6, if prompts are used, extend them or add separate ideas.
Notice how these messages match the mark scheme. The mark scheme gives marks for what students show they can do, and the examiner reports show where students lose marks.

ex.t: Turn the key messages into a poster
b: Write each message as one short sentence in your students' words.
Put it on the classroom wall.
Refer to it every time you mark a past paper exercise.

x7.h: What the June 2024 examiner report says about Exercises 1 and 3
p: The examiner report for June 2024 Paper 11 gives exact reasons why students lost marks. Use these when you teach the exercises.
Exercise 1 (the cosplay article). The exercise was generally well attempted.
• Question 1: some chose the distractor, 1939. Most noticed that 'created' in the text matches 'invented' in the question.
• Question 2: most students matched 'I'd choose' in the text with 'prefer' in the question and picked 'fantasy'. Very few picked 'science fiction', the distractor.
• Question 3: harder. Many answers left out the key word 'World' from 'World Cosplay Summit', which was needed to show the global event, not a local or regional one.
• Question 4: well done. Students saw that 'role' in the text and 'type of character' in the question mean the same.

• Question 5: students must read the whole paragraph. Some chose 'selling cosplay costumes' from the first sentence, but that was about 'lots of people', not the person in the question. The correct response was 'taking photographs'.
• Question 6: most students gained all marks. A mark could not be given if the comparative 'more' in point three was left out.
Exercise 3 (car-free cities notes). The exercise was answered successfully by most students.

• Question 8: some notes were incomplete. 'Charging drivers' needed 'to enter parts of the city'. 'Parking charges' needed 'outside the workplace'. 'Public transport' alone did not show improvement, so 'better' was needed.
• Question 9: all four options were found. Students used verbs such as 'renting', 'sharing' and 'downloading'. 'Using a mobile phone' was not precise enough for 'downloading an app'.

Notes from Paper 12 Exercise 1: common wrong answers came from students who did not read beyond the first information (for example, 'the hard protective shell'). Some included extra wrong details such as 'close to the surface', which cost the mark.

b: Teach students to circle key words in every question (World, more, better, outside the workplace).
Practise answers that are precise and short.
Give notes tasks where the heading decides which verb or detail is needed.
Practise reading the whole paragraph before choosing an answer.

x8.h: What the June 2024 examiner report says about Exercises 2 and 4
p: Exercise 2 (wild swimming matching, Paper 11). Students did best on (b) and (d), and many also got (a), (c), (e) and (h). Questions (f), (g) and (i) were harder.

• (f): the statement 'whatever the weather' matched only text D ('it does not matter how cold or wet it is'). Many chose B because of a nearby sentence about winter, but that was qualified by 'it's only when it's too windy...'.

• (g): the statement 'suggests that a memory might have been inaccurate' matched text C. Students may have chosen A because 'remembered' linked to 'memory', but A was a definite, clear remembrance. The key word was 'suggests'.

• (i): 'suggests that they have done something risky' matched a sentence in text D ('I have been the only one there... not a good idea'). Many chose C. The key word 'suggests' meant looking for an implied idea.
Teaching idea: have students mark the key word in each statement and ask 'Is this a fact or an implied idea?'.
Exercise 4 (ToddlerLab article, Paper 11). Many students gained full marks. Questions 11, 12 and 15 were easier. Questions 10, 13 and 14 were harder.
• Question 10: the key word 'suggests' showed implied meaning. Option C was wrong because the text said the child was 'simply part of a group'.
• Question 13: students needed the first stage of the process. The key word 'begins' and the word 'then' made clear that watching a recording came first.
• Question 14: the key word was 'research', which meant the aim over a longer time, not what happened in one session.

From Paper 12, Question 7 (matching poems): many students gained at least four marks. Students should check that the text fully supports their answer and look for rephrasing, not repeated words. Some left questions blank or gave the same answer to all.

b: Underline words like 'suggests', 'begins', 'research' and 'whatever'.
Ask: what does this word tell me to look for?
Practise finding the sentence that answers the key word.
Do not accept a choice made only because one word matches.

x9.h: What the June 2024 examiner report says about Exercises 5 and 6
p: Exercise 5 (an email about a sports event, Paper 11). Most students made a good attempt, with an informal tone and all three bullet points.
Strong responses:
• Described the event in detail with time and place, and gave their own interest.
• Gave a believable reason for helping and a full explanation of what they would do.
• Added opinions and feelings, such as how tiring a job might be.
• Wrote as to a real friend with natural phrases (for example, a question asking if the friend agrees).
Weaker responses:
• Listed sports with no detail, or described only the rules of a sport.
• Gave only one short reason for helping.
• Used very formal language such as 'I would like to inform you' (better in Exercise 6).

Language slips: mixing past and present, and confusing 'take place' and 'take part'. Spelling was generally good, with errors such as 'price' for 'prize' and 'exited' for 'excited'. Some answers had only short, simple sentences with no clauses or connectives.
Exercise 6 (a magazine review, Paper 11). Students wrote in a suitably formal tone. Strong responses:
• Gave balanced comments on good and bad qualities.
• Used a range of complex structures and less common vocabulary.
• Used cohesive expressions appropriately, such as 'it's worth noting that' and 'having said that'.
• Wrote a concluding paragraph with different words from the main body.
Weaker responses told only the story line, copied the four prompts, gave only price information or described magazines in general rather than reviewing one.

b: Content: did the writer address every bullet and develop the ideas?
Language: is there a range of structures and vocabulary, with accuracy?
Register: friendly in Exercise 5 and formal in Exercise 6.
Avoid copying prompts.

x9.h: Extra marking practice: the 2024 specimen writing tasks
p: Use the two specimen tasks for more practice.

Question 16 (Exercise 5). You recently bought an item online and there was a problem with it. Write an email to a friend. Explain why you bought it, describe the problem and say what you are going to do. Write about 120 to 160 words.

Question 17 (Exercise 6). Your class took part in a one-day sports festival for local schools. Write a report for the organisers saying what was enjoyable and suggesting how it could be improved. Comments: a chance to meet students from other schools; there were not many new sports to try; I learned a lot about fitness; we spent too much time listening to instructions. Write about 120 to 160 words.

Mark each answer using Table A (Content, out of 6) and Table B (Language, out of 9). The specimen mark scheme says for both tables: marks 5 to 6 for Content when the task is fulfilled, content is fully relevant, the style is consistently appropriate and ideas are very well developed; 7 to 9 for Language for skilful communication, a wide range of vocabulary and structures, high accuracy, effective organisation and a wide range of linking words.
Use your own students' work or write a sample at Level 4 and Level 6 to practise marking. Then compare marks with a colleague.

b: Paragraph 1: why I bought it.
Paragraph 2: the problem.
Paragraph 3: what I will do.
Friendly start and ending.

x10.h: What the June 2024 examiner report says about Listening
p: The June 2024 examiner report for the Speaking Endorsement syllabus includes a report on a listening paper. These points are useful for any listening class.
Exercise 1 (eight short recordings, picture options). Students did very well on most questions.

• Question 5: some chose option A, the sport the speaker already played, but the question asked about the new sport she wanted to try, which was football. Students must listen to which idea the question targets.
• Question 7: some picked D. Students may be less familiar with phrases for decisions and comparisons.
Exercise 2 (two multiple-choice questions per recording). Students did well on questions about feelings, attitudes and opinions.
• Question 13: some chose A, tempted by the word 'brother' in the recording and 'relative' in the option.
• Question 17: some chose C because they took 'Really?' as agreement.
• Question 11: only about half answered correctly. 'I suddenly heard a bang in the engine' links to the option 'It made a loud noise', which students did not link.
• Question 15: only half were correct. Many chose the two distractors.

Exercise 3 (a talk about bats, eight statements). Most students did very well. Question 25: some chose 'high-pitched' or 'noisy' because they heard similar adjectives. Question 26: some chose 'guided walks' because of the word 'tours', while the correct option used 'talks' for presentations.
Exercise 4 (multiple matching on long-distance train travel, six short monologues). The statements covered opinions, evaluations and preferences.

b: Teach students to listen for the idea, not just the word.
Practise paraphrase: 'bang in the engine' means 'loud noise'.
Teach phrases for decisions and comparisons.
After each exercise, play the recording with the script and mark where the answer is.

x13.h: What the June 2024 teacher's notes add: rules for the day
p: The Paper 3 Teacher's/Examiner's Notes for May/June 2024 have clear rules. Know them well, because they protect fairness.
Before the tests:
• Make sure there is a quiet room and that recording equipment works.
• The Speaking Assessment cards must not be opened until one working day before the test. Cards and notes must stay confidential and be kept in a secure place until the end of the examination period.
On the day:
• Record every test in full, without stopping or pausing.
• Hold the test in English from start to finish.
• Use a suitable room with exam conditions. Supervise candidates so that those leaving do not speak to those waiting.
• Nobody else should be in the room except another teacher or examiner, a moderator or a Cambridge representative.
• The examiner, not the candidate, chooses the card before the candidate comes in.
• No notes, no dictionaries and no written notes during the test.
• Candidates may ask for clarification at any time.
• The examiner sits facing the candidate with a table between them and does not let the candidate see the examiner's notes.
Recording:
• Start each recording with the examiner's name, candidate number, candidate name and date. End by saying 'end of recording'.
• Check audibility before and during the session, and make spot checks before submission.
• Name each track with the candidate number and name, and use a separate track for each candidate.

b: Room and recorder tested.
Cards unopened until one working day before.
Opening statement ready.
Files named with number and name.

x13.h: Helping a student who stops, and extension prompts
p: The notes give exact words you may use. Follow them.

Part 2, if the candidate does not start speaking after about 15 seconds: 'Are you ready to start talking about the points on the card?' After another 5 seconds: 'Would you like to tell me about the options on the card?' If the candidate still does not start, say 'Thank you. Can I have the card back, please? Now let's move on to Part 3 of the test.'
If a candidate starts but cannot continue, ask: 'Is there anything else you would like to say?' and then move on to Part 3.

To get more from a candidate in Part 1 and Part 3: 'Can you tell me more about ...?' 'Can you tell me why ...?' 'Can you explain what you mean ...?' 'Can you give me any examples of ...?' If a candidate has very little to say after prompts, move on.

What to avoid: distracting the candidate; interrupting with your own views or correcting mistakes; showing impatience or surprise; giving the idea that there are right answers; and using phrases such as 'well done' or 'that was very good'.

b: Objective: do not let what you know about the student's personality change the marks.
Positive: give credit for what the student can do. First-language level is not required for top marks in a criterion.
Consistent: apply the criteria the same way to all students so the rank order is reliable.

x13.h: What the June 2024 examiner report says about marking Speaking
p: Examiners saw patterns in the marking by centres.

• Grammar: generally accurate. Some centres were slightly generous when students spoke naturally but with a narrow range of structures. The overall tendency was to be generous in the upper marks, perhaps because the teacher knew the student's general ability. Some marking was slightly severe when examiners focused too much on small errors.

• Vocabulary: generally accurate, but with a tendency to be generous for repeated technical words rather than precise, appropriate words. In the lower range some centres were slightly severe, and could credit collocations and fixed expressions more.

• Development: credit for developing and structuring responses. Some centres were severe with weaker candidates and generous to stronger ones. Sometimes quantity of speech was marked generously even when not relevant.

• Pronunciation: many centres did not mark it as a stand-alone criterion. The mark was often matched to the other criteria. Some examiners marked too severely for accent, even if pronunciation was clear and intonation was used well.

Administration: recordings were mostly good, but sometimes students were too far from the microphone or rustling paper and air conditioning covered their voices. Some centres made errors copying marks onto the Speaking Examination Summary Form, so check carefully and use an electronic form where possible.
Internal moderation must be done if more than one examiner is used. The lead examiner should listen to a range of candidates (top, middle and bottom) from each examiner.

b: Pick two recordings: one fluent but simple, one hesitant but clear.
Mark all four criteria separately.
Discuss if you were generous or severe.

x15.h: Where to place specimen and past papers in your year map
p: Add papers to your year map so they do not appear suddenly at the end.
• Term 1: use the 2024 specimen Paper 1 to show students the format. Do one exercise as a class, with the answers, as a model.
• Term 2: use past paper exercises (one exercise at a time) after teaching each skill, and mark with the mark scheme.
• Term 3: run full timed mocks for Paper 1 and Paper 2, and a recorded speaking mock for Paper 3.
• Final weeks: use the examiner reports to target common errors, and revise.
Keep these dates inside your exam buffer of 6 to 8 weeks so that teaching and revision both fit.

b: Do not wait until the last term to show a past paper.
Do not use only past papers. Students also need real reading and listening.

x18.h: Using the specimen reading text as a diagnostic
p: You can use a short exercise from the 2024 specimen Paper 1 as part of your diagnostic test. For example, Exercise 1 (the article about living stone plants, with six short questions for 8 marks) tests whether students can find specific facts and follow simple advice. It is a good way to see their reading level.
How to use it:
• Give students 15 minutes alone, with no help.
• Mark with the specimen mark scheme (the answers are in Unit 27).
• Record who scored 0 to 3, 4 to 6 and 7 to 8.
• Group students by results and plan reading support.
Remember that the aim of the diagnostic is to understand needs, not to give a grade.

b: Low score and few answers: check vocabulary and basic reading.
Medium score: practise precise answers and key words.
High score: stretch with Exercise 2 and Exercise 4 skills.
